transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, thank you for fitting me in. I just... I really didn't know what else to do at this point. I came in because for the past few weeks, I’ve just felt this... this incredibly heavy, sad pressure sitting on me. It's almost like a physical weight, you know? And it's there almost all day long, from the minute I wake up. 

I try so hard to shake it off, especially because of my job. I'm a nurse, an LPN, so I'm constantly around people who need me to be strong and positive. I go into work and I'm doing my rounds, and I'm putting on this big, bright smile for my patients, asking them how they're doing, making sure they're comfortable... but inside, I feel like I’m barely holding myself together. It takes so much energy just to keep that smile up when all I feel is this deep, sinking sadness. I keep thinking it'll pass if I just focus on my shift, or if I just keep busy with the charts and the patients, but the pressure just stays right there, pressing down on me. Even when I'm right in the middle of talking to someone and acting completely normal, I feel like I'm just one minor thing away from completely falling apart, and it's exhausting to live like this every single day...
Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy?

No, not really. And honestly, that's a big part of what's scaring me right now, because I used to have this whole routine to keep myself balanced. Being an LPN, you know, you're on your feet all day, dealing with so much emotional and physical stuff from the patients, so I always made sure I had outlets to decompress after my shifts. I used to come home and paint—I have this little corner in my living room set up with my easel and all my acrylics, and I could just lose myself in it for hours. Or I'd go to a hot yoga class, which was amazing for my back after lifting people all day, or even go salsa dancing on Thursday nights with my girlfriends. We had this regular spot we’d go to, and it was just... it was fun. It felt so good to just move and laugh and feel like myself outside of the clinic. 

But lately... I don't know, the idea of doing literally any of that just seems completely impossible. I'll finish my shift, and the second I get to my car, all I can think about is just getting through the front door of my apartment. I just go home, and I don't even change out of my scrubs half the time. I just sit down on the couch and kind of stare into space. My friends will text me, asking if I'm coming to salsa or if I want to grab a spot next to them in yoga, and my phone will just light up on the coffee table, and I just look at it. I end up ignoring all their texts because even the thought of typing out a reply, let alone actually going out, feels like this massive mountain I have to climb. None of it feels worth the effort anymore. I look at my paints sitting right there in the corner and I just feel completely blank. There's no spark, no joy in the idea of doing it. I just sit there on the couch wasting my whole evening until it's time to go to sleep, because I just can't bring myself to care about the things I used to love.
Do you often feel guilty or blame yourself for things?

No, not really... I mean, I don't think I walk around feeling guilty about things, at least not in the way you're asking. I know some people get really down on themselves and blame themselves for every little thing that goes wrong, but I don't really have that going on. I'm just... I'm just so tired and sad all the time. 

Like, at work, I don't feel like I'm making mistakes or doing a bad job that I should feel guilty about. I know I'm still doing my job as a nurse, I'm still giving the meds on time, I'm still doing the wound care properly... I just feel empty while I'm doing it. And with my friends, I mean, I feel bad that I'm ignoring their texts, sure, but it's not this deep, overwhelming guilt that eats away at me. It's more just... I know I should reply, I know they're probably wondering where I am, but I just literally don't have the energy to care enough to feel guilty about it, if that makes sense? 

It's strange, because normally I'm the kind of person who hates letting people down. Like, if I had to cancel plans a few months ago, I would have sent a long text apologizing and trying to reschedule right away because I'd feel terrible about it. But now? Now it's just this blankness. I see the text, I know I'm flaking, and I just... I just let the screen go dark and stare back at the wall. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm sitting around blaming myself or feeling a lot of guilt. It's more like I just don't have enough feeling left inside me to even muster up guilt right now. Everything just feels too heavy and flat for that.
Have you been having any problems with your sleep?

Sleep? Um, no, not really. I mean, I guess my sleep is pretty much the same as it's always been. I don't think I'm having any real problems with it, not that I've noticed anyway. 

I usually try to get to bed around 10:30 or 11:00 because my shifts start so early, you know? As an LPN, I have to be at the clinic, clocked in, and ready for handover by 7:00 AM sharp, which means my alarm goes off at 5:30. And I've always been pretty good at sticking to that schedule. Even now, with everything feeling so heavy and awful, I still manage to get into bed at my normal time. I'll do my whole nighttime routine—well, most of it anyway, sometimes I skip washing my face if I'm just too exhausted—but I get under the covers, and I usually fall asleep okay. 

And I'm not waking up in the middle of the night or tossing and turning for hours or anything like that. I just sleep through until my alarm goes off. Sometimes I think maybe I'm sleeping a little deeper just because I'm so incredibly drained from pretending to be okay all day at work, but I'm definitely getting my normal seven or eight hours. It's just... even when I wake up after a full night's sleep, I don't feel rested. I hear the alarm, and I just lay there looking at the ceiling, feeling that exact same heavy pressure sitting on my chest before I've even swung my legs out of bed. But the actual sleeping part? No, I wouldn't say I'm having any problems with that. I'm just sleeping my normal amount and waking up feeling just as bad as when I went to sleep.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite lately?

Yeah, actually... my appetite has definitely changed. I mean, I know I should be eating regularly, I really do. Being a nurse, I'm literally the one lecturing my patients all day about nutrition and making sure they're getting enough calories, especially when they're struggling. So I know how important it is, especially right now when everything just feels so draining. But honestly... most days, food just sounds completely unappealing to me. 

Like, the idea of eating a full meal just makes me feel almost repulsed, or it just seems like way too much effort to even figure out what to eat, let alone chew and swallow it. I used to be so good about it, too. I'd meal prep on Sundays and pack these nice salads or chicken and rice in my little lunch bag for work, but lately, I don't pack anything at all. I'll get to the clinic, and we get so busy with the morning rush—rooming patients, doing vitals, updating charts, dealing with the doctors—that I don't even think about food. My stomach doesn't even rumble. 

And then I'll realize, usually halfway through my shift, like around 1 or 2 in the afternoon when I finally sit down at the nurses' station for a second to catch my breath, that I haven't eaten a single real thing. I'll look back at my morning and realize I've literally only had a couple of dry saltine crackers from the breakroom stash and, like, three cups of black coffee. And even then, I only eat the crackers because my stomach starts feeling sour and acidic from all the coffee, not because I actually have an appetite. My coworkers will be passing around a menu to order takeout for lunch, or someone will bring in bagels, and they'll ask if I want anything, and I just wave them off. I just can't bring myself to eat because nothing sounds good. Even when I get home at night, like I was saying before about just sitting on the couch in my scrubs, I don't even bother making dinner. I might eat a piece of toast or something just so I don't wake up feeling sick, but the actual desire to eat a meal is just completely gone.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual?

Yeah, um... actually, yes. It's funny you bring that up because I was just realizing this the other day at work. Everything I do right now just feels so... slowed down. It's like I'm moving through syrup, if that makes sense? Like there's this thick, heavy resistance against every single movement I try to make. 

Even just the really simple things at the clinic that I usually do on autopilot. Like, gathering wound care supplies. Normally, I can zip into the supply closet, grab the saline, the 4x4 gauze, the paper tape, maybe some barrier cream, and be back in the patient's room in, like, thirty seconds flat. My hands just know where everything is. But lately? I walk in there, and it's like my arms weigh a hundred pounds each. I just stand there for a second, and the actual physical act of reaching up to the shelf, pulling the boxes down, getting the supplies together... it just takes me noticeably longer than it should. It's almost like my brain is sending the signal to my muscles to move, but the message is getting delayed somewhere along the way. 

And it’s the exact same thing with my charting. As a nurse, you know, documentation is literally half the job. If it’s not charted, it wasn’t done. I used to be so fast at it. I’d sit down at the workstation, pull up the system, and just type out my progress notes and vitals in a couple of minutes between rooming patients. But now, finishing charting feels like this monumental task. I'll sit down at the keyboard, and my fingers just feel sluggish. I’m staring at the screen, and I know exactly what I need to say, but the actual typing is just so slow. It takes me so much longer to finish charting a basic follow-up visit than it ever used to. 

And even when I'm talking, like right now, or when I'm explaining discharge instructions to a patient... I feel like I'm dragging my words out, or taking these longer pauses because it just takes too much energy to speak at my normal pace. It’s just this constant, exhausting drag on my whole body, all day long. Everything just takes so much longer.
Have you been having any thoughts about harming yourself?

Harming myself? Um... no. No, I don't have any kind of plan to hurt myself or anything like that. I really want to be clear about that. But... well, it’s actually the whole reason I finally asked for help. I was at my prenatal appointment recently—I'm pregnant, which is supposed to be this huge, happy thing, right? And I was sitting there in the exam room waiting for the doctor, and I just sort of realized how bad things had gotten in my head. 

Because even though I would never actively do anything to end my life, I’ve been having these thoughts... these really dark, heavy thoughts where I just go to bed at night and I catch myself wishing that I just wouldn't wake up. Like, I'll be lying there, staring at the ceiling like I told you about earlier, and I just think, wouldn't it be so much easier if my alarm went off at 5:30 and I just... wasn't here anymore? If I could just stay asleep forever and not have to keep dragging myself through every single day. 

And having that thought... it just terrified me. It scared me so much because, you know, I have a baby on the way, I have a life, I have my patients, but I still have this overwhelming desire to just slip away in my sleep. It felt so wrong and so frightening to feel that way while pregnant. That’s what scared me enough to finally say something to my OB at that prenatal appointment. I just couldn't keep it to myself anymore. I told her that I don't want to hurt myself, I have absolutely no plan to do that, but I just constantly wish I wouldn't wake up in the morning. So... yeah. No active plans to cause harm, but those thoughts are definitely there, and they're just really hard to live with.
How many weeks have you been feeling this heavy, sad pressure?

Um... let me think. It’s been... yeah, it’s been about three weeks now. I know the exact timeline because it started right after I found out I was pregnant. Like, almost immediately after. 

I remember taking the test, and you know, you always see in movies or hear from other people that when you see that positive result, you're supposed to feel this overwhelming wave of excitement, or maybe just normal nervousness about having a baby. But for me, just a couple of days after I got that positive result, this... this huge, heavy cloud just kind of descended on me. And it hasn't lifted since. 

I kept trying to rationalize it at first, honestly. Being a nurse, my brain immediately goes to the clinical side of things, so I was telling myself, 'Okay, your hormones are shifting, your HCG is rising, progesterone is going up, it's just a normal physiological response, you're just emotional from the early pregnancy changes.' I really, really tried to convince myself it was just that, just a normal first-trimester thing that would pass in a few days. But it’s been a solid three weeks now, and it’s not just normal pregnancy mood swings. It's this constant, suffocating weight that I just can't shake. Every single day for the last three weeks, ever since that test, it's just been sitting there right on my chest.
Have you been feeling restless or having trouble sitting still?

Restless? No, no, not restless. Honestly, it’s the exact opposite of that. Like I was saying a minute ago, I'm just... I'm so slow. Everything I do feels slowed down, like I’m literally moving through syrup. I don't have the energy to be restless or fidgety. 

It's just that heavy, dragging feeling I mentioned. Like, even just sitting here right now, I don't feel the urge to move or get up or pace around or anything. I just feel stuck. Like I was saying about the clinic, you know, with the wound supplies and the charting... it's all just taking me noticeably longer than it should because my body just doesn't want to move. It's like I have to force every single motion. So, no, definitely not restless. Just... weighed down. Everything is just so much effort.
Do you feel like you're able to concentrate on things as well as you used to?

Concentrate? Oh, definitely not. Not at all. It's actually becoming a real problem, especially at work. Like, I’ll be looking at a patient’s chart, right? And I keep having to reread the same medication orders over and over again. Or the wound-care notes—I'll read them, and it’s like the words are just floating on the page and not actually entering my brain. My head just feels so incredibly foggy all the time. 

And it’s not just reading things; it’s making decisions, too. Things that I usually do on autopilot, without even having to think about them—like adjusting a dressing or deciding the best time to administer a PRN med—now, I just freeze. I stand there and I second-guess every single little thing I do. I’ll think, 'Wait, did I double-check that dose? Should I use the hydrocolloid or the foam dressing?' And I *know* the answers, I’ve done this a thousand times, but my brain just stalls out. It’s like there’s this thick wall between me and my own knowledge. I’ll just stand in the supply room staring at the shelves, completely blanking on what I went in there for. It’s so frustrating, and honestly, it’s scary, because I’m a nurse, you know? I can’t afford to be making mistakes or second-guessing myself when it comes to patient care, but I just can't seem to focus on anything for more than a few seconds before my mind just drifts off into this heavy fog again.
Do you often feel worthless or like you're not a good person?

Worthless? I mean... I don't know if I'd use the word worthless, exactly. Or that I'm a bad person. I don't think I'm a bad person. But... I definitely feel like I'm failing right now. Like, really failing. Especially with the pregnancy, you know? 

Like I was saying, this is supposed to be this magical time, and I just feel so disconnected and empty. And then I start thinking, 'What kind of mother is going to feel this way?' You know? Like, my baby is growing inside me right now, and instead of feeling joy or love or even just normal anticipation, I just feel this crushing weight and this fog. And then the guilt sets in. Oh my gosh, the guilt is just awful. I lay in bed at night—when I'm not staring at the ceiling, anyway—and I just beat myself up over it. I think about how unfair it is to the baby, how unfair it is to my husband, who is actually excited, bless him. He's trying so hard to be supportive, and I'm just a lump on the couch. 

And then that spills over into work. Like I was telling you about the charting and the meds... I start feeling like a terrible nurse, too. I've worked so hard for my license, I went through all that schooling, and now I can't even remember if I grabbed the right gauge needle without checking it three times. So it's this spiral. I feel bad about the pregnancy, which makes me feel like a bad mom already, and then I feel bad about work, which makes me feel like a bad nurse, and it all just kind of piles up. But... worthless? No, I don't think I'm completely worthless. I just... I just feel like I'm doing a really terrible job at everything right now. Like I'm letting everyone down, including myself. It's just... it's a lot of guilt. But I wouldn't say I feel like a fundamentally bad person. Just... broken right now, I guess.
Have you been feeling fidgety or having an urge to pace back and forth?

Fidgety? Um... I feel like we kind of just touched on this, right? With the restlessness? But no, absolutely no pacing at all. I really don't have the energy to pace or fidget. 

Like I was trying to explain a few minutes ago, it’s honestly the exact opposite. Everything I do feels slowed down. It’s literally like I’m moving through syrup. Every single physical movement takes so much effort right now. I know I mentioned the clinic earlier, but it really shows up there... even simple things, like gathering wound supplies. Usually, I can just dart into the supply closet, grab the kerlix, the barrier cream, the tape, whatever I need, and be out in five seconds flat because I know exactly where everything is. But now? It's like my arms weigh a hundred pounds each just reaching up to the shelves. I'm just physically dragging. 

And finishing my charting... it takes me noticeably longer than it should. What used to be a quick twenty-minute wrap-up at the end of my shift drags on forever, not just because of the brain fog I was talking about, but because my hands literally just don't want to type at a normal speed. I'm just sitting there at the computer station, moving in slow motion. So yeah, definitely no urge to pace back and forth. If I could just sit in one chair all day and never have to physically get up or move my body, I'd probably do it, because fighting through that heavy, syrupy feeling is just exhausting.
Have you experienced any significant weight loss or gain since you started feeling this heavy, sad pressure?

Weight? Um... well, the thing is, with the pregnancy, you're supposed to be gaining weight, right? Like, that's the whole goal. You go to the OB, they put you on the scale, they chart the progress. But honestly... I don't even know what my weight is doing right now because my eating is just completely messed up. 

I know I should be eating regularly. I really do. Especially now, with the baby. The doctor gave me this whole packet on nutrition and how many extra calories I need, and my husband bought all these healthy snacks to keep around the house. But... I just can't. Most days, food just sounds completely unappealing. Like, the thought of actually preparing a meal, or even just chewing something, just feels like too much work. It's like that syrupy feeling I was talking about with moving around? It applies to eating, too. 

And it's really bad at work. I'll be halfway through a clinic shift, you know, dealing with the wound care and the charting and just trying to keep my head above water with the brain fog, and I'll suddenly realize it's 2 PM and all I've had all day is a handful of saltine crackers or maybe just a cup of coffee. And even then, the coffee is mostly just because it's warm and I can just sip it without having to actually eat anything. 

My husband gets so worried. He'll make dinner, and he tries to make things he knows I usually love, like this chicken pasta bake he does, but I'll sit down at the table and just push it around my plate. I take maybe two bites and I'm just done. The appetite just isn't there. It's completely gone. And then, of course, that brings back all the guilt I was talking about earlier, because I know I'm not giving the baby what it needs, but I physically just cannot force myself to eat when everything tastes like cardboard and my stomach just feels like a tight knot. So, as for actual weight loss or gain... I guess I'm probably not gaining what I should be, but I'm almost too afraid to look at the scale at this point because I know it's just going to be one more thing I'm failing at right now.
Have you been feeling an intense urge to engage in activities that you normally enjoy, or to do things that might be considered reckless or impulsive?

Reckless? Or doing things I enjoy? Oh, gosh, no. No, not at all. I mean, honestly, the idea of doing anything I normally enjoy just sounds exhausting right now. Like, before all this started, I used to love going to this little pottery studio down the street on my days off. It was my way to decompress after a long week at the clinic, you know? Just getting my hands dirty, focusing on the clay, not thinking about wound care or charting or any of that. My husband actually bought me a whole package of classes for my birthday last year, and I think I still have like four left. But the thought of going now... it just feels like a chore. Like, I'd have to get dressed, drive there, actually try to be creative and make something, and talk to the instructor... I just don't have it in me. 

And as for reckless or impulsive things... no, definitely not. Like I said, I'm barely eating and I feel like I'm moving through syrup all day. The last thing I want to do is anything wild or impulsive. I don't even have the energy to go grocery shopping, let alone do something reckless. I just want to stay in my house, on the couch, where it's quiet and I don't have to pretend to be okay. Even when my husband suggests something small, like just going for a walk around the neighborhood or grabbing a decaf coffee at the drive-thru, I usually just tell him I'm too tired. 

So, no, there's no intense urge to do anything, really. The only urge I have is to just lie down and sleep, even though I know I'll probably just lay there staring at the ceiling and feeling guilty about not doing anything. It's just this constant feeling of wanting to retreat from everything. So, no reckless behavior. No sudden urges to take up skydiving or max out the credit cards or anything like that. Just... nothing. Just that heavy, empty feeling I was talking about.
Have you been feeling like you need to keep moving or doing something all the time?

Moving all the time? Oh, um... no. Actually, I feel like we might have talked about this a little bit already, right? With the pacing and the restlessness? Because, honestly, it's the exact opposite of needing to keep moving. I don't have the energy to keep moving. I don't have the energy to do much of anything. 

Like I was trying to explain before, everything I do just feels incredibly slowed down. It's literally like I'm moving through syrup, or like my body is made of lead, and every single physical movement takes so much effort right now. Even at the clinic, where I'm usually so fast and efficient. Like, I used to pride myself on being the nurse who could get a room turned over and prepped for the next patient in under three minutes. But now? Even simple things, like gathering wound supplies... it's just exhausting. Usually, I can dart into the supply closet, grab the kerlix, the barrier cream, the tape, and be out in five seconds flat because I know exactly where everything is. But now, it's like my arms weigh a hundred pounds each just reaching up to the shelves. I'm just physically dragging my feet down the hallway. 

And finishing my charting... oh, my gosh, it takes me noticeably longer than it should. What used to be a quick twenty-minute wrap-up at the end of my shift drags on forever. I'm just sitting there at the computer station, moving in slow motion, staring at the screen, and my hands literally just don't want to type at a normal speed. It's so frustrating because I know the other nurses are waiting on me to finish so we can all give report and leave, but I just can't make my body move any faster. So, no, definitely no feeling of needing to keep moving. If anything, I just want to stop moving completely.
Do you find yourself fidgeting or feeling an internal restlessness that makes you want to move around?

Fidgeting? No, not at all. I know I just mentioned this, but it really is the exact opposite. I don't have any internal restlessness or urge to move around. In fact, it's just... it's like I was just saying, everything I do feels so incredibly slowed down. 

It's really hard to explain unless you've felt it, but it's literally like I'm moving through syrup all day long. Every movement takes this massive amount of effort. Even at the clinic, where I'm usually, you know, constantly on my feet and moving fast. I'm a vocational nurse, so I'm used to a fast pace. But lately, even the simplest things take me noticeably longer than they should. Like, I was just talking about gathering the wound supplies... it's just a simple task, right? You walk in, you grab the gauze, the tape, whatever you need, and you walk out. But now, it's like my legs are filled with lead just walking to the supply room, and my arms feel so heavy when I reach up to grab things. 

And the charting... oh my gosh, the charting. It's the same thing. It takes me so much longer than it used to. I sit there at the computer, and my fingers just don't want to type at a normal speed. It's like the connection between my brain and my hands is just lagged, you know? It's not just that I'm tired, it's a physical heaviness, a physical slowness. So, no, there's no fidgeting. There's no pacing or restlessness. If I could just sit still and not move a single muscle all day, I probably would, because moving just feels like such a monumental task right now. It's just this constant, heavy slowness in everything I do.
Do you find yourself unable to sit still due to feeling anxious or agitated?

Anxious or agitated to the point where I can't sit still? Oh, wow. I feel like... I mean, I know we just went over this, right? With the fidgeting and the restlessness? Because, really, I have to say again, it's the exact opposite of that. I'm not agitated or anxious in a way that makes me want to move. I don't want to move at all. 

Like I was trying to explain, and I know I'm probably repeating myself, but it's just so overwhelming... everything I do is just so incredibly slowed down. It's that feeling of moving through syrup. That's the best way I can describe it. It's not just being tired; it's this profound, physical heaviness. Even the most basic things at the clinic, things I could do in my sleep before, are taking me so much longer than they should. I mentioned gathering the wound supplies, right? It used to be this quick, fluid motion. Walk in, grab the gauze, the tape, the saline, out the door. Now, it's like every step is a conscious effort, and reaching my arm up to the shelf feels like lifting weights. 

And the charting... I know I brought that up too, but it's just such a glaring example of how slow I am right now. Sitting at the computer, trying to type out my notes, and my fingers just will not move at their normal speed. It's like my brain is sending the signal, but my hands are taking their sweet time getting the message. It's noticeably longer. Everyone can see it. So, no, there's absolutely no inability to sit still. If anything, sitting still is the only thing I feel capable of doing. The idea of being agitated and pacing around... I just don't have the physical energy for it. Everything is just slow, heavy, and exhausting.
Do you find yourself feeling an overwhelming need to be active and do things, like you can't calm down?

An overwhelming need to be active? Like I can't calm down? I... I really don't mean to be difficult, but I feel like we keep circling back to the exact same thing, and I'm just not sure how else to say it. I really, truly do not have any extra energy or any urge to be active. It is the complete and total opposite. 

I know I've said this like three times now, but it's just so frustrating because it's dominating my entire life right now. Everything I do feels so incredibly slowed down. I just... I don't have this nervous energy you're asking about. I have zero energy. It's that feeling I keep mentioning, like I'm moving through thick syrup all day. Every step, every movement, it's just heavy. 

Like I was explaining about work at the clinic—and I know I keep bringing up work, but it's where I notice it the most because I'm usually so on top of things as a nurse—even the most basic tasks are just dragging. Gathering wound supplies, which used to be completely automatic, now it's like I have to force my body to walk to the supply room, force my arm to reach out for the gauze and the tape. It takes me noticeably longer than it should. And my charting... I sit there and my hands just feel like lead on the keyboard. It takes me forever to type up a simple note that used to take me two minutes. Everyone else is finishing up and I'm just stuck there, moving in slow motion. 

So, no, I definitely don't feel like I can't calm down or that I need to be active. I feel like I'm already too calm, too slow, too heavy. If I could just lie down and not move for a week, I would. I just don't have it in me to be active right now.
Do you find yourself feeling an intense need to engage in constant physical activity?

Constant physical activity? Doctor, I... I'm sorry, I really don't mean to be rude, but are you listening to me? I feel like I'm losing my mind here because you keep asking me variations of the exact same question, and I keep giving you the exact same answer. I just... I don't understand why we keep coming back to this idea that I'm bouncing off the walls or needing to move constantly. 

I literally just spent the last ten minutes explaining that I have zero energy for *any* activity, let alone constant physical activity. I'm going to say it again, and I really, really hope it makes sense this time, because I don't know how else to explain it. Everything—literally every single thing I do from the moment I wake up—feels completely, overwhelmingly slowed down. It is the absolute furthest thing from needing to be active. It’s that syrup feeling I keep mentioning. I am moving through thick, heavy syrup all day long. 

I work in a clinic. I'm a nurse. I am supposed to be fast and efficient, but right now, even the most mundane, simple things are taking me noticeably longer than they ever should. I go to the supply closet to gather wound supplies—something I've done a million times, just grabbing some gauze and some medical tape—and it feels like I'm running a marathon just to lift my arms. I sit down at the end of my shift to finish my charting, and my fingers just drag across the keyboard like they weigh ten pounds each. It's humiliating, honestly, because I know people are noticing how sluggish I am. So, no. No intense need for physical activity. None. It's a complete, physical inability to move at a normal speed, and it's exhausting just trying to get through a single shift.
Do you have a plan for how you would harm yourself if you were to act on those thoughts of not wanting to wake up?

No, no, I don't have a plan. I really don't. I... I know I just got a little frustrated with all the questions about moving around, and I'm sorry about that, it's just been a long day, but... no, to answer your question, I don't have a plan to hurt myself. 

It's more just... well, it's actually what finally pushed me to say something. I was at my prenatal appointment, and you know how they always ask you those screening questions? Usually, I just brush right past them, but this time... I don't know, it just kind of hit me. I realized that lately, I've been having these thoughts. Not about doing something to myself, not like that, but just... this feeling of wishing I wouldn't wake up. Like, going to sleep and just hoping the morning doesn't come because everything is just so heavy and slow and exhausting right now.

Being an LPN, you know, you're on your feet all day, dealing with so much emotional and physical stuff from the patients, so I always made sure I had outlets to decompress after my shifts. I used to come home and paint—I have this little corner in my living room set up with my easel and all my acrylics, and I could just lose myself in it for hours. Or I'd go to a hot yoga class, which was amazing for my back after lifting people all day, or even go salsa dancing on Thursday nights with my girlfriends. We had this regular spot we’d go to, and it was just... it was fun. It felt so good to just move and laugh and feel like myself outside of the clinic. 

But lately... I don't know, the idea of doing literally any of that just seems completely impossible. I'll finish my shift, and the second I get to my car, all I can think about is just getting through the front door of my apartment. My friends will text me, asking if I'm coming to salsa or if I want to grab a spot next to them in yoga, and my phone will just light up on the coffee table, and I just look at it. I end up ignoring all their texts because even the thought of typing out a reply, let alone actually going out, feels like this massive mountain I have to climb. None of it feels worth the effort anymore. I look at my paints sitting right there in the corner and I just feel completely blank. There's no spark, no joy in the idea of doing it. Like, at work, I don't feel like I'm making mistakes or doing a bad job that I should feel guilty about. I know I'm still doing my job as a nurse, I'm still giving the meds on time, I'm still doing the wound care properly... I just feel empty while I'm doing it. And with my friends, I mean, I feel bad that I'm ignoring their texts, sure, but it's not this deep, overwhelming guilt that eats away at me. It's more just... I know I should reply, I know they're probably wondering where I am, but I just literally don't have the energy to care enough to feel guilty about it, if that makes sense?

Like, if I had to cancel plans a few months ago, I would have sent a long text apologizing and trying to reschedule right away because I'd feel terrible about it. But now? So, no, I wouldn't say I'm sitting around blaming myself or feeling a lot of guilt. It's more like I just don't have enough feeling left inside me to even muster up guilt right now. As an LPN, I have to be at the clinic, clocked in, and ready for handover by 7:00 AM sharp, which means my alarm goes off at 5:30. And I've always been pretty good at sticking to that schedule. Even now, with everything feeling so heavy and awful, I still manage to get into bed at my normal time. I'll do my whole nighttime routine—well, most of it anyway, sometimes I skip washing my face if I'm just too exhausted—but I get under the covers, and I usually fall asleep okay.

Sometimes I think maybe I'm sleeping a little deeper just because I'm so incredibly drained from pretending to be okay all day at work, but I'm definitely getting my normal seven or eight hours. It's just... even when I wake up after a full night's sleep, I don't feel rested. I hear the alarm, and I just lay there looking at the ceiling, feeling that exact same heavy pressure sitting on my chest before I've even swung my legs out of bed. But the actual sleeping part? No, I wouldn't say I'm having any problems with that. I'm just sleeping my normal amount and waking up feeling just as bad as when I went to sleep.

patient.answer:
Yeah, um... actually, yes. It's funny you bring that up because I was just realizing this the other day at work. Everything I do right now just feels so... slowed down. Even just the really simple things at the clinic that I usually do on autopilot. Like, gathering wound care supplies. Normally, I can zip into the supply closet, grab the saline, the 4x4 gauze, the paper tape, maybe some barrier cream, and be back in the patient's room in, like, thirty seconds flat. I’d sit down at the workstation, pull up the system, and just type out my progress notes and vitals in a couple of minutes between rooming patients. But now, finishing charting feels like this monumental task. I'll sit down at the keyboard, and my fingers just feel sluggish. I’m staring at the screen, and I know exactly what I need to say, but the actual typing is just so slow. It takes me so much longer to finish charting a basic follow-up visit than it ever used to. 

And even when I'm talking, like right now, or when I'm explaining discharge instructions to a patient... I feel like I'm dragging my words out, or taking these longer pauses because it just takes too much energy to speak at my normal pace. It’s just this constant, exhausting drag on my whole body, all day long. Everything just takes so much longer.

Because even though I would never actively do anything to end my life, I’ve been having these thoughts... these really dark, heavy thoughts where I just go to bed at night and I catch myself wishing that I just wouldn't wake up. Like, I'll be lying there, staring at the ceiling like I told you about earlier, and I just think, wouldn't it be so much easier if my alarm went off at 5:30 and I just... wasn't here anymore? It scared me so much because, you know, I have a baby on the way, I have a life, I have my patients, but I still have this overwhelming desire to just slip away in my sleep. Worthless? I mean... I don't know if I'd use the word worthless, exactly. Or that I'm a bad person. I don't think I'm a bad person. But... I definitely feel like I'm failing right now. Like, really failing. Especially with the pregnancy, you know? 

Like I was saying, this is supposed to be this magical time, and I just feel so disconnected and empty. And then I start thinking, 'What kind of mother is going to feel this way?' You know? Like, my baby is growing inside me right now, and instead of feeling joy or love or even just normal anticipation, I just feel this crushing weight and this fog. And then the guilt sets in. Oh my gosh, the guilt is just awful. I lay in bed at night—when I'm not staring at the ceiling, anyway—and I just beat myself up over it. I think about how unfair it is to the baby, how unfair it is to my husband, who is actually excited, bless him. He's trying so hard to be supportive, and I'm just a lump on the couch. 

And then that spills over into work. Like I was telling you about the charting and the meds... I start feeling like a terrible nurse, too. I've worked so hard for my license, I went through all that schooling, and now I can't even remember if I grabbed the right gauge needle without checking it three times. So it's this spiral. I feel bad about the pregnancy, which makes me feel like a bad mom already, and then I feel bad about work, which makes me feel like a bad nurse, and it all just kind of piles up. But... worthless? No, I don't think I'm completely worthless. I just... I just feel like I'm doing a really terrible job at everything right now. Like I'm letting everyone down, including myself. It's just... it's a lot of guilt. But I wouldn't say I feel like a fundamentally bad person. Just... broken right now, I guess.

doctor.question: Have you been feeling like you need to keep moving or doing something all the time?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: Everything I do feels slowed down, like I’m moving through syrup, and even simple things at the clinic like gathering wound supplies or finishing charting take me noticeably longer than they should.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the need to keep moving or doing something all the time, which assesses for psychomotor agitation, a component of psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Moving all the time? Oh, um... no. Actually, I feel like we might have talked about this a little bit already, right? With the pacing and the restlessness? Because, honestly, it's the exact opposite of needing to keep moving. I don't have the energy to keep moving. I don't have the energy to do much of anything. 

Like I was trying to explain before, everything I do just feels incredibly slowed down. It's literally like I'm moving through syrup, or like my body is made of lead, and every single physical movement takes so much effort right now. Even at the clinic, where I'm usually so fast and efficient. Like, I used to pride myself on being the nurse who could get a room turned over and prepped for the next patient in under three minutes. But now? Even simple things, like gathering wound supplies... it's just exhausting. Usually, I can dart into the supply closet, grab the kerlix, the barrier cream, the tape, and be out in five seconds flat because I know exactly where everything is. But now, it's like my arms weigh a hundred pounds each just reaching up to the shelves. I'm just physically dragging my feet down the hallway. 

And finishing my charting... oh, my gosh, it takes me noticeably longer than it should. What used to be a quick twenty-minute wrap-up at the end of my shift drags on forever. I'm just sitting there at the computer station, moving in slow motion, staring at the screen, and my hands literally just don't want to type at a normal speed. It's so frustrating because I know the other nurses are waiting on me to finish so we can all give report and leave, but I just can't make my body move any faster. So, no, definitely no feeling of needing to keep moving. If anything, I just want to stop moving completely.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation
doctor.question: Do you find yourself fidgeting or feeling an internal restlessness that makes you want to move around?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: Everything I do feels slowed down, like I’m moving through syrup, and even simple things at the clinic like gathering wound supplies or finishing charting take me noticeably longer than they should.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about fidgeting or internal restlessness, which refers to psychomotor agitation, a component of psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Fidgeting? No, not at all. I know I just mentioned this, but it really is the exact opposite. I don't have any internal restlessness or urge to move around. In fact, it's just... it's like I was just saying, everything I do feels so incredibly slowed down. 

It's really hard to explain unless you've felt it, but it's literally like I'm moving through syrup all day long. Every movement takes this massive amount of effort. Even at the clinic, where I'm usually, you know, constantly on my feet and moving fast. I'm a vocational nurse, so I'm used to a fast pace. But lately, even the simplest things take me noticeably longer than they should. Like, I was just talking about gathering the wound supplies... it's just a simple task, right? You walk in, you grab the gauze, the tape, whatever you need, and you walk out. But now, it's like my legs are filled with lead just walking to the supply room, and my arms feel so heavy when I reach up to grab things. 

And the charting... oh my gosh, the charting. It's the same thing. It takes me so much longer than it used to. I sit there at the computer, and my fingers just don't want to type at a normal speed. It's like the connection between my brain and my hands is just lagged, you know? It's not just that I'm tired, it's a physical heaviness, a physical slowness. So, no, there's no fidgeting. There's no pacing or restlessness. If I could just sit still and not move a single muscle all day, I probably would, because moving just feels like such a monumental task right now. It's just this constant, heavy slowness in everything I do.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation
doctor.question: Do you find yourself unable to sit still due to feeling anxious or agitated?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: Everything I do feels slowed down, like I’m moving through syrup, and even simple things at the clinic like gathering wound supplies or finishing charting take me noticeably longer than they should.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor agitation (inability to sit still, feeling anxious or agitated), which falls under psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Anxious or agitated to the point where I can't sit still? Oh, wow. I feel like... I mean, I know we just went over this, right? With the fidgeting and the restlessness? Because, really, I have to say again, it's the exact opposite of that. I'm not agitated or anxious in a way that makes me want to move. I don't want to move at all. 

Like I was trying to explain, and I know I'm probably repeating myself, but it's just so overwhelming... everything I do is just so incredibly slowed down. It's that feeling of moving through syrup. That's the best way I can describe it. It's not just being tired; it's this profound, physical heaviness. Even the most basic things at the clinic, things I could do in my sleep before, are taking me so much longer than they should. I mentioned gathering the wound supplies, right? It used to be this quick, fluid motion. Walk in, grab the gauze, the tape, the saline, out the door. Now, it's like every step is a conscious effort, and reaching my arm up to the shelf feels like lifting weights. 

And the charting... I know I brought that up too, but it's just such a glaring example of how slow I am right now. Sitting at the computer, trying to type out my notes, and my fingers just will not move at their normal speed. It's like my brain is sending the signal, but my hands are taking their sweet time getting the message. It's noticeably longer. Everyone can see it. So, no, there's absolutely no inability to sit still. If anything, sitting still is the only thing I feel capable of doing. The idea of being agitated and pacing around... I just don't have the physical energy for it. Everything is just slow, heavy, and exhausting.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation
doctor.question: Do you find yourself feeling an overwhelming need to be active and do things, like you can't calm down?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: Everything I do feels slowed down, like I’m moving through syrup, and even simple things at the clinic like gathering wound supplies or finishing charting take me noticeably longer than they should.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about an overwhelming need to be active or inability to calm down, which refers to psychomotor agitation, a component of psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
An overwhelming need to be active? Like I can't calm down? I... I really don't mean to be difficult, but I feel like we keep circling back to the exact same thing, and I'm just not sure how else to say it. I really, truly do not have any extra energy or any urge to be active. It is the complete and total opposite. 

I know I've said this like three times now, but it's just so frustrating because it's dominating my entire life right now. Everything I do feels so incredibly slowed down. I just... I don't have this nervous energy you're asking about. I have zero energy. It's that feeling I keep mentioning, like I'm moving through thick syrup all day. Every step, every movement, it's just heavy. 

Like I was explaining about work at the clinic—and I know I keep bringing up work, but it's where I notice it the most because I'm usually so on top of things as a nurse—even the most basic tasks are just dragging. Gathering wound supplies, which used to be completely automatic, now it's like I have to force my body to walk to the supply room, force my arm to reach out for the gauze and the tape. It takes me noticeably longer than it should. And my charting... I sit there and my hands just feel like lead on the keyboard. It takes me forever to type up a simple note that used to take me two minutes. Everyone else is finishing up and I'm just stuck there, moving in slow motion. 

So, no, I definitely don't feel like I can't calm down or that I need to be active. I feel like I'm already too calm, too slow, too heavy. If I could just lie down and not move for a week, I would. I just don't have it in me to be active right now.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation
doctor.question: Do you find yourself feeling an intense need to engage in constant physical activity?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: Everything I do feels slowed down, like I’m moving through syrup, and even simple things at the clinic like gathering wound supplies or finishing charting take me noticeably longer than they should.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor agitation or hyperactivity (intense need for constant physical activity), which falls under the category of psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Constant physical activity? Doctor, I... I'm sorry, I really don't mean to be rude, but are you listening to me? I feel like I'm losing my mind here because you keep asking me variations of the exact same question, and I keep giving you the exact same answer. I just... I don't understand why we keep coming back to this idea that I'm bouncing off the walls or needing to move constantly. 

I literally just spent the last ten minutes explaining that I have zero energy for *any* activity, let alone constant physical activity. I'm going to say it again, and I really, really hope it makes sense this time, because I don't know how else to explain it. Everything—literally every single thing I do from the moment I wake up—feels completely, overwhelmingly slowed down. It is the absolute furthest thing from needing to be active. It’s that syrup feeling I keep mentioning. I am moving through thick, heavy syrup all day long. 

I work in a clinic. I'm a nurse. I am supposed to be fast and efficient, but right now, even the most mundane, simple things are taking me noticeably longer than they ever should. I go to the supply closet to gather wound supplies—something I've done a million times, just grabbing some gauze and some medical tape—and it feels like I'm running a marathon just to lift my arms. I sit down at the end of my shift to finish my charting, and my fingers just drag across the keyboard like they weigh ten pounds each. It's humiliating, honestly, because I know people are noticing how sluggish I am. So, no. No intense need for physical activity. None. It's a complete, physical inability to move at a normal speed, and it's exhausting just trying to get through a single shift.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of suicidal thoughts with a plan
doctor.question: Do you have a plan for how you would harm yourself if you were to act on those thoughts of not wanting to wake up?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: What scared me enough to say something at my prenatal appointment was that I’ve been having thoughts like I wish I just wouldn’t wake up, even though I don’t have a plan to hurt myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal ideation and whether I have a plan to harm myself, which directly maps to the Death_Suicide symptom.

patient.answer:
No, no, I don't have a plan. I really don't. I... I know I just got a little frustrated with all the questions about moving around, and I'm sorry about that, it's just been a long day, but... no, to answer your question, I don't have a plan to hurt myself. 

It's more just... well, it's actually what finally pushed me to say something. I was at my prenatal appointment, and you know how they always ask you those screening questions? Usually, I just brush right past them, but this time... I don't know, it just kind of hit me. I realized that lately, I've been having these thoughts. Not about doing something to myself, not like that, but just... this feeling of wishing I wouldn't wake up. Like, going to sleep and just hoping the morning doesn't come because everything is just so heavy and slow and exhausting right now. 

And it really scared me. It scared me enough that I actually brought it up to the OB-GYN, which is a big deal for me because I usually just keep my head down and push through. But having a thought like that, especially right now... it just felt wrong. But I want to be really clear, because I know how these things sound—I'm a nurse, I know the drill—I don't have any intention of acting on it. There's no plan, no... no method or anything like that. It's just this passive, lingering wish that I could just stop for a while. Just not wake up and have to face how hard it is to just put one foot in front of the other. But no, no plan to actually harm myself. I promise you that.
